# **1\. Dataset and Protocol**

## **1.1 Data source**

Images were collected from two real-world sources, a lost-items folder and a found-items folder, each containing 447 images, for a combined dataset of 894 images. Using both sides of the lost-and-found interaction is important: it means the classifier sees the same categories of objects photographed by different people under different lighting, angles, and backgrounds. This diversity makes the model more robust and less likely to overfit to a single visual style.

## **1.2 Model classification**

Six everyday item categories were selected that are commonly left behind in public spaces: bag, charger, handkerchief, lunchbox, tumbler, and wallet. These categories were chosen because they represent the most frequently reported lost items and are visually distinct enough for a model to learn, yet similar enough (e.g., bag vs. lunchbox, charger vs. wallet in terms of size) to make the classification non-trivial.

## **1.3 Figure 1: Dataset Distribution**

**![][image1]**

*Figure 1\. Left: Total images per category across the full 894-image dataset. Right: Balanced split between lost-updated (green) and found-updated (red) sources within each category.*

The left bar chart shows the overall count per class. Tumbler (218) and bag (196) dominate, while the other four classes are tied at 120 each. The right grouped chart confirms that for every class, the lost and found sources contribute almost exactly equal numbers, this parity is deliberate: it ensures that the model cannot learn to distinguish classes simply by recognizing visual cues tied to one source folder.

## **1.4 Data Splitting**

The dataset was divided into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) subsets using a stratified split.

A stratified split means that the class proportions are preserved in each subset. This prevents a situation where, for example, all tumbler images end up concentrated in training and the validation set never sees one. 

The resulting sizes are 625 training, 134 validation, and 135 test images. The test set is held out entirely during training and is only used once at the very end to report final performance, this gives an unbiased estimate of how well the model generalizes to truly unseen data.

The validation accuracy stays high and even slightly above training accuracy, which is normal since the main model is still frozen and stable. Around the unfreeze point, there’s a noticeable drop in training accuracy and a spike in loss, but this is expected because more layers are being updated. After that, the model recovers and both accuracy and loss stabilize. Since the training and validation results stay close to each other, it shows that the model is performing well and not overfitting.

# **3\. Test Performance**

## **3.1 Overall Metrics**

After all training phases were complete, the model was evaluated once on the held-out test set of 180 images, these images it had never seen during training or validation.

**Table 1: Overall Test Performance of the Lost-and-Found Item Classifier (n=180 test images, 6 categories)**

| Metric | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Top-1 Accuracy | 91.67% |
| Top-3 Accuracy | 99.44% |
| Cross-Entropy Loss | 0.2767 |

 

A federated deep learning study using MobileNetV2 for three-class chest X-ray classification achieved 88% accuracy with an F1-score of 89.66% (Hassan et al., 2026\) close to the 91.67% Top-1 accuracy as seen on table 4.1, and on a similarly constrained dataset. A comprehensive MobileNetV2 study on visual field defect classification reported an overall MobileNetV2 accuracy of 97.84% (PMC, 2022), but this was achieved on a well-structured medical imaging dataset with visually distinct categories and high-quality images making conditions considerably more favorable than real-world, user-photographed lost items against cluttered backgrounds. A wildlife image classification benchmark using ResNet50 reported a highest accuracy of 90.3% (Gonzalez-Mendoza et al., 2024\) on images with occlusions, varying lighting, and motion blur, a setting directly similar to ours thus confirming that 88–91% represents the realistic performance ceiling for lightweight CNN classifiers under genuine real-world conditions with limited training data. The Top-3 accuracy of 98.52% is an especially strong result: it means that for virtually every lost item query, the correct category appears within the model's top three predictions. The cross-entropy loss of 0.2767 further confirms that the model is not merely guessing correctly, it is assigning high probability mass to the correct class, meaning its confidence is well-calibrated and not spread thinly across multiple categories. 

## **3.2 Table 1: Per-Class Precision, Recall, and F1**

 

| Class | Precision | Recall | F1-Score | Support |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Bag | 1.00 | 0.90 | 0.95 | 30 |
| Charger | 0.94 | 0.97 | 0.95 | 30 |
| Handkerchief | 1.00 | 0.93 | 0.97 | 30 |
| Lunchbox | 0.92 | 0.80 | 0.86 | 30 |
| Tumbler | 0.88 | 0.93 | 0.90 | 30 |
| Wallet | 0.81 | 0.97 | 0.88 | 30 |
| Macro Avg. | 0.92 | 0.92 | 0.92 | 180 |
| Weighted Avg. | 0.92 | 0.92 | 0.92 | 180 |

 

The macro-averaged F1 of 0.92 and weighted F1 of 0.92 are strong results for a six-class problem with just few training images. For reference, a MobileNetV2-based framework for multi-label remote sensing image classification achieved a highest F-beta score of 0.9275, outperforming all other tested architectures including Vision Transformer, ResNet-50, Inception-v3, and DenseNet-121 (Sethi et al., 2024\) and this was on a dataset of over 40,000 images. Even with lesser training and test dataset the model still achieved the same score. F1 combines precision and recall into one score, balancing both. It penalizes models that are good at one but bad at the other. In a retrieval system, this matters because low precision shows irrelevant results, while low recall means the correct item might not appear at all. The per-class F1 pattern here is favorable because the weakest class (wallet, F1 \= 0.88) still performs well, and the strongest classes (handkerchief, F1 \= 0.97) confirm that the model has learned genuinely reliable representations for the most distinctive item types. The precision-recall gap for charger and bag (high precision, lower recall) is consistent with the general finding that in a strictly supervised setting, models tend to perform best on classes with clear inter-class margins and high intra-class consistency (Hav4ik, 2021).

*Figure 3\. Confusion matrix on the 180-image test set. Rows are true labels; columns are predicted labels. Darker diagonal cells indicate correct classifications.*

The confusion matrix shows strong overall performance, achieving an overall accuracy of 91.67%, with most predictions correctly falling along the diagonal. For bags, there are 27 true positives, 3 false negatives, and 0 false positives, meaning the model identifies bags reliably with no incorrect “bag” predictions. Charger has 29 true positives, 1 false negative, and 2 false positives, indicating very high accuracy with a few instances where other items were predicted as chargers. The lunchbox class is where the model struggles most, with 24 true positives, 6 false negatives, and 2 false positives, reflecting confusion especially with similar container-like objects. Tumbler shows 28 true positives, 2 false negatives, and 4 false positives, meaning some non-tumblers were incorrectly predicted as tumblers. Lastly, wallet achieves 29 true positives and only 1 false negative but has the highest false positives at 7, suggesting the model sometimes over-predicts this class when features overlap with other compact items.

 **5\. Retrieval Demonstration**

**(Why 10 (add a reference or a paper that backing why i should get the top 10)Add reference inline citation**

Using three sample lost items: a bag, a handkerchief, and a charger. For each query image taken from the lost-items folder, the system computes a hybrid similarity score for every image in the found-items folder and returns the top 10 ranked matches. The hybrid score is computed as: score \= (1 − color\_w) × embedding\_similarity \+ color\_w × color\_similarity, where color\_w \= 0.28. Background suppression is enabled (suppress\_bg \= True) to ensure that color comparisons reflect the object itself rather than the surrounding environment. Each result reports the mixed score (mix), the raw embedding similarity (emb), the color similarity (col), the predicted category, and the pair ID that identifies the true matching item.

![][image4]Ranking: (1-color\_w)\*embedding \+ color\_w\*color\_sim  |  color\_w=0.28  suppress\_bg=True

The retrieval system correctly identifies all ten results as bags, confirming strong category-level discrimination. The top match (pair=bag\_01) achieves the highest combined score (mix \= 0.8092), driven largely by a very high color similarity (col \= 0.9029), suggesting the found bag closely matches the color of the lost one. Some results show high embedding similarity but lower color scores like the 8th result with (emb \= 0.7832, col \= 0.5709), which likely correspond to bags with a similar shape and texture but different colors. The consistent retrieval of same category items across all ten positions confirms that the embedding space has learned a meaningful representation of bag features.

The handkerchief query yields the strongest retrieval performance of the three demonstrations. The true matching item, it is ranked first with a mix score of 0.8637, and all ten results are correctly identified as handkerchiefs. Both the embedding and color components are consistently high across the list, reflecting the visually distinctive nature of handkerchiefs, which tend to have recognizable patterns, textures, and colors. This result is consistent with the perfect recall (1.00) observed for the handkerchief class in the classification evaluation, indicating that the model has learned a robust and reliable representation for this category.

For the charger query, color similarity is the dominant driver of the ranking, with most results achieving color scores above 0.90. This reflects the typically uniform and neutral color of chargers (white or black), making color a strong differentiating cue within the category. Notably, the true matching item ranks fourth (mix \= 0.7770) rather than first, with three other chargers ranked above it. This indicates that while the system reliably retrieves the correct category, distinguishing between specific instances within a visually homogeneous class remains challenging. Nevertheless, the true match still surfaced within the top four results, which would be sufficient for a user reviewing a short candidate list. As chargers can look very similar to each other.

# **5	SUMMARY, CONCLUSIONS, AND RECOMMENDATIONS**

## **5.1	Summary**

This study introduces a multi-phase transfer learning pipeline designed to automate the identification of commonly lost items such as bag, charger, handkerchief, lunchbox, tumbler, and wallet. This was done using a dataset of 894 real-world images collected from the web.

Training proceeded in three phases using MobileNetV2 as the backbone. Phase 1 established a strong baseline (91.04% validation accuracy) by training only the classification head on frozen ImageNet features. Phase 2 refined higher-level representations through selective backbone fine-tuning, raising validation accuracy to 91.79%. Phase 3 introduced metric learning via batch-hard triplet loss to produce a compact 128-dimensional embedding space, followed by softmax head retraining that achieved a peak validation accuracy of 92.54%.

Using the test set of 135 images, the final model achieved a Top-1 accuracy of 88.89%, Top-3 accuracy of 98.52%, a macro mAP of 0.9705, and a cross-entropy loss of 0.3405. Per-class results were consistently strong, with handkerchief and tumbler showing the highest F1 scores, and wallet and bag presenting the most confusion.

.

## **5.2	Conclusions**

This work demonstrates that a carefully structured three-phase transfer learning approach can achieve strong image classification performance on a modest domain-specific dataset. The progressive nature of the training moving from frozen feature extraction through selective fine-tuning to metric learning addresses the core challenge of adapting large pretrained networks to small datasets without overfitting.

The model’s Top-3 accuracy of 98.52% and macro mAP of 0.9705 are particularly significant for a retrieval application: in a real lost-and-found system, presenting users with the top three matching categories covers virtually every test case correctly. The introduction of triplet loss in Phase 3 adds a meaningful retrieval-oriented dimension beyond standard classification, enabling similarity-based search that could support future use cases such as image-to-image matching between lost and found queries.

The primary limitation of this study is dataset scale. With 894 images across six categories, the model has limited exposure to the full range of visual appearances each category can exhibit. Future work should focus on expanding the dataset, particularly for bags and wallets, which showed the most inter-class confusion.

## **5.3	Recommendations**

# 5.3.1 Dataset Expansion

# It is recommended to expand the dataset to at least 300–500 images per class, with priority given to bag and wallet categories, which currently exhibit the most misclassification. Additional images should be collected under varied lighting conditions, orientations, and backgrounds to improve model robustness. Data augmentation techniques (random rotation, color jitter, horizontal flip) should be applied during training to further increase effective dataset diversity.

# 5.3.2 Model Deployment

# Given MobileNetV2’s lightweight architecture, the model is suitable for deployment as a mobile or web-based lost-and-found assistant. It is recommended to expose the Top-3 predictions rather than the Top-1 result in the user interface, as the Top-3 accuracy of 98.52% provides near-complete coverage. A confidence threshold should be applied: predictions below \[PLACEHOLDER: e.g., 60%\] softmax confidence should prompt the user to provide additional details rather than returning a low-confidence match.

# 5.3.3 Future Research Directions

# Future iterations of this system should explore: (1) image-to-image retrieval using the Phase 3 embedding space, enabling direct matching between a lost item photo and found item photos without requiring category selection; (2) extension to additional item categories beyond the current six; (3) integration of text metadata (item descriptions, location, date) alongside image embeddings for a multimodal retrieval system; and (4) continual learning strategies that allow the model to incorporate new categories or images without full retraining.

# **5\. Limitations and Future Work**

## **5.1 Single Split**

All metrics are reported from a single 70/15/15 stratified split. A more rigorous evaluation would use k-fold cross-validation, running the entire training pipeline five times with different splits and averaging the results. A single split can produce either optimistic or pessimistic estimates depending on which images happen to fall in the test set.

## **5.2 Class Imbalance**

Bag (196) and tumbler (218) are over-represented relative to the other four classes (120 each). This means the model has seen more diversity for those classes during training, which partly explains their stronger F1 scores. Future work could augment the minority classes with synthetic transforms (rotation, color jitter, cutout) or apply class-weighted loss during training to compensate.

## **5.3 Test Set Size**

With only 135 test images (as few as 18 per class for the smaller categories), confidence intervals on per-class metrics are wide. For example, a single additional correct classification in 'charger' would raise its recall from 0.78 to 0.83. A larger dataset, especially for the less common categories, would give more stable estimates.

## **5.4 Retrieval Beyond Classification**

Phase 3 (triplet loss embeddings) opens the door to image-level retrieval — matching a submitted photo of a lost item against a database of found items without requiring the user to select a category. This capability was demonstrated qualitatively in the notebook but not evaluated quantitatively here. Future work should compute retrieval mAP and rank-1 accuracy on a held-out retrieval benchmark.

# Tab 4

To make this more human and easier to explain, think of the three phases as the **"Educational Journey"** of your AI. You aren't just dumping data into a box; you are teaching it like a student—starting with the basics and moving toward specialized expertise.

Here is a breakdown of why each phase exists, humanized for clarity:

---

### **Phase 1: The "Broad Education" (Baseline)**

**The Goal:** Give the model a steady start without "breaking" what it already knows.

* **Why we did it:** Imagine your AI is a graduate student who already knows everything about general photography (ImageNet). In Phase 1, we "freeze" its brain and only teach it to recognize your 6 specific categories.  
* **The Benefit:** Since we only trained the very last layer (the "decision maker"), the model couldn't overthink or get confused. It quickly learned the obvious differences between a charger and a tumbler. It’s like a person learning to sort mail into 6 bins—they don’t need to know how paper is made yet; they just need to see the labels.

### **Phase 2: The "Specialist Training" (Fine-Tuning)**

**The Goal:** Help the model notice the subtle, "real-world" details of lost items.

* **Why we did it:** A bag doesn't always look like a perfect studio photo. In Phase 2, we "unfroze" the deeper layers of the AI's brain. This allowed the model to adjust its vision to match your specific dataset (the lighting in the lost-and-found bin, the angles of a dropped wallet).  
* **The Benefit:** This is where the model stops looking at "general shapes" and starts looking at "textures and specific details." This small adjustment pushed the accuracy higher because the model became a specialist in *your* items, not just general objects.

### **Phase 3: The "Memory Palace" (Metric Learning)**

**The Goal:** Teach the model to understand *relationships*, not just labels.

* **Why we did it:** Sometimes a wallet looks like a bag, or a charger looks like a tangled mess. Standard training just says "This is a Wallet." In Phase 3, we used **Triplet Loss**. We showed the model three images at a time:  
  1. An "Anchor" (a specific wallet).  
  2. A "Positive" (another wallet).  
  3. A "Negative" (a bag).  
* **The Benefit:** We forced the model to pull "like" items together and push "unlike" items far away in its mental map (the 128-D space). This created a "Memory Palace" where every category has its own distinct neighborhood. By the time we retrained the final classifier, the model didn't just guess; it *understood* exactly how a wallet is different from a bag.

---

### **Why this 3-Step process is better than just 1:**

If you had tried to do all of this at once, the model would likely have "catastrophically forgotten" its previous knowledge or become overwhelmed by the small dataset (894 images).

By doing it in phases, you:

1. **Stabilized** it first (Phase 1).  
2. **Sharpened** its vision (Phase 2).  
3. **Organized** its memory (Phase 3).

**The Result:** A system that doesn't just guess correctly 88% of the time on the first try but is so well-organized that the right answer is almost **always (98.5%)** in its "Top 3" list—making it incredibly reliable for a human user searching for their lost stuff.

How do you feel about using the "Educational Journey" analogy for your project?

## **1\. Why "Last 70" Layers? (Phase 2 Fine-Tuning)**

MobileNetV2 has 154 layers. We chose to unfreeze exactly the **last 70** for a strategic reason: **The Hierarchy of Features.**

* **The Bottom Layers (1–84):** These layers are "Feature Extractors." They see basic things like lines, circles, and colors. Since your items (bags, tumblers) are made of the same lines and colors as the 1.2 million images in ImageNet, these layers are already perfect. Changing them would be a waste of time and could actually make the model worse (**Catastrophic Forgetting**).  
* **The Top Layers (85–154):** These layers are "Concept Extractors." They combine lines and circles into complex objects like "the handle of a bag" or "the spout of a tumbler."  
* **The "70" Decision:** By unfreezing roughly the top half of the network, we gave the model enough "brain capacity" to redefine complex shapes specifically for lost-and-found items, while keeping the foundational "vision" (the bottom 84 layers) locked and stable. This prevents **overfitting**—where the model memorizes your specific photos instead of learning the general idea of the object.

---

## **2\. Why a 128-Dimensional Embedding? (Phase 3\)**

In Phase 3, we stopped asking the model "What is this?" and started asking "How similar are these?" We converted every image into a list of 128 numbers (an embedding).

* **Why 128?** It’s the "Goldilocks" number of dimensions.  
  * If it were too small (e.g., 8 or 16), the model wouldn't have enough "room" to represent the complex differences between a leather wallet and a fabric pouch.  
  * If it were too large (e.g., 1024), the model would become too "picky," creating a map that is so sparse it fails to find patterns (the **Curse of Dimensionality**).  
  * **128** provides enough mathematical space to cluster items clearly while remaining computationally fast for a mobile-friendly model like MobileNetV2.

---

## **3\. Why "Batch-Hard" Triplet Loss?**

Standard training just looks at one image at a time. Triplet loss looks at three: an **Anchor**, a **Positive** (same class), and a **Negative** (different class).

* **The "Batch-Hard" Reasoning:** Most triplets are "easy"—for example, the model easily knows a bright red tumbler is not a black leather wallet. If the model only sees easy examples, it stops learning.  
* **The Solution:** "Batch-Hard" forces the model to look through the current batch of images and find the **hardest** examples: the two wallets that look the most different and the wallet and bag that look the most similar.  
* **The Result:** This forces the model to "sweat" during training, focusing only on the most confusing cases. This is why your **Top-3 accuracy** is so high (98.5%)—the model has been specifically trained to distinguish between lookalikes.

---

## **4\. Why Retrain the Softmax Head? (Phase 3b)**

After Phase 3, the model's "internal map" changed completely because of the Triplet Loss.

* **The Reasoning:** The classification head from Phase 2 was trained to look at the *old* map. If we didn't retrain it, the "decision-maker" would be using an outdated GPS.  
* **The Benefit:** By retraining just the final Softmax layer on top of these new, highly-organized 128-D embeddings, we combined two powers:  
  1. The model's ability to **cluster** similar items (from Triplet Loss).  
  2. The model's ability to **label** those clusters (from Softmax).  
* This "Double-Check" is what pushed your accuracy from **91.79%** to your peak of **92.54%**.

---

## **Summary of the Engineering Logic**

| Decision | Technical Reason | Human Benefit |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Frozen Backbone** | Preserves "General Vision" | Prevents the AI from "forgetting" how to see. |
| **Last 70 Layers** | Refines "Object Logic" | Helps the AI see the difference between a lunchbox and a bag. |
| **128-D Space** | Optimal Feature Density | Makes the search fast but very accurate. |
| **Batch-Hard Loss** | Discriminative Learning | Trains the AI to handle "trick" items that look similar. |
| **Softmax Retrain** | Alignment | Ensures the final "label" matches the new "internal map." |

**Discussion**

**6.1 Overall System Performance**

The results across all evaluation stages demonstrate that the proposed system achieves strong performance on the lost-and-found item classification and retrieval task. The final test accuracy of 88.89% and Top-3 accuracy of 98.52% indicate that the model is both accurate and well-calibrated, making it practically viable in a real-world deployment where a user could review the top few results to confirm a match. The macro mAP of 0.9705 further confirms that the model ranks the correct class near the top of its confidence list for nearly every test query, which is the most critical property for a retrieval-oriented system.

The three-phase training strategy proved effective. Phase 1 feature extraction rapidly established a strong baseline (91.04% validation accuracy), Phase 2 fine-tuning refined higher-level representations (91.79%), and Phase 3 metric learning with triplet loss further improved the quality of the embedding space, culminating in a Phase 3b softmax accuracy of 92.54%. Each phase built upon the last without catastrophic forgetting, validating the phased approach for small domain-specific datasets.

**6.2 Class-Level Strengths and Weaknesses**

Among the six categories, tumbler and handkerchief consistently emerged as the strongest performers. Tumbler benefited from having the largest number of training samples (218 total), which gave the model more opportunities to learn its distinctive cylindrical shape. Handkerchief, despite having only 120 samples, achieved perfect recall (1.00) on the test set, likely due to its unique fabric texture and folded appearance, which are visually distinct from the other five categories. These results suggest that even with limited data, visually distinctive items can be learned reliably.

Bag and charger showed the largest gaps between precision and recall. Bag’s high visual variability, spanning different shapes, sizes, materials, and colors, makes it inherently harder to classify consistently. Some bag images were confused with lunchboxes and wallets, pointing to inter-class visual overlap for boxy or rectangular objects. Charger and wallet share thin, rectangular form factors, leading to mutual confusion in the classification results. These error patterns are intuitive and consistent with real-world visual ambiguity, rather than random misclassification.

**6.3 Effectiveness of the Hybrid Retrieval Approach**

The hybrid ranking formula that combines embedding similarity with color histogram similarity (color weight \= 0.28) addresses a known limitation of embedding-only retrieval: two items of the same category but different colors can be near-indistinguishable in the embedding space. By incorporating color as a secondary signal, the system can differentiate between, for example, a red bag and a black bag that share similar shape features. The retrieval demonstrations confirm this: for handkerchiefs and chargers, the color component played a decisive role in surfacing the correct match or closely related items at the top of the ranked list.

Background suppression (suppress\_bg=True) is another important component of the pipeline. Lost and found item photos are typically taken in diverse, cluttered environments, and without suppressing the background, the color histogram would capture irrelevant environmental colors rather than the object’s own color. This preprocessing step ensures the color similarity score reflects the item itself, making the hybrid score more reliable across varying photographic conditions.

**6.4 Limitations**

Despite the strong overall metrics, several limitations remain. First, the dataset is relatively small at 894 images across six categories, and the class imbalance between tumbler and bag (218 and 196 samples, respectively) versus the other four classes (120 each) may cause the model to generalize less well to underrepresented categories under more varied conditions. Second, the system is limited to six predefined item categories. In a real deployed lost-and-found system, items outside these categories, such as keys, umbrellas, or electronics, would not be handled correctly. Extending the category set would require additional labeled data and retraining.

Third, while the retrieval demonstration shows that the true match is always found within the top 10 results, it is not always ranked first. For the charger query, the true pair ranked fourth. In a high-volume lost-and-found system with many candidate images, even a rank-4 result could be buried among a large list, reducing user experience. Finally, the color weight (0.28) was set empirically and may not generalize optimally to all categories or lighting conditions; a learned or adaptive weighting scheme could improve performance.

**6.5 Recommendations for Future Work**

Future work could address these limitations in several ways. Expanding the dataset through data augmentation techniques such as random cropping, color jitter, and horizontal flipping, or through web scraping additional real-world images, would improve class balance and model robustness. Introducing an open-set recognition mechanism, where the model can detect and flag items that do not belong to any known category, would make the system more practical for real-world deployment. Additionally, replacing the fixed color weight with a learned attention or fusion module could allow the model to dynamically balance embedding and color signals depending on the query item type. Finally, user studies evaluating whether the top-3 or top-5 retrieval results are sufficient for end users to identify their lost items in a real institutional setting would provide valuable real-world validation of the system.

 

# Tab 8

In a MobileNetV2 model, the numerical values of extracted features do not correspond to a single, easily named human concept like "roundness" or "redness." Instead, they represent activation strengths—a measure of how strongly a specific learned pattern is present at a particular location in the image.   
Medium  
Medium  
 \+1  
What the Numbers Represent  
Activation Level: A higher numerical value in a feature map indicates that the specific filter in that layer "saw" a strong match for the pattern it was trained to detect.  
Pattern Matching: Each filter is a matrix of learned weights. When the filter slides over an image (convolution), it performs a mathematical match. If the image patch matches the filter's pattern, the output value is high; if it doesn't match, the value is low or zero.  
Spatial Mapping: Because feature maps are 2D grids, the position of a high numerical value tells the model where in the image that specific feature was found.
